items.title: Editorials
Review of Low Back Pain
items.summary: To the Editor A recent Review synthesized articles on nonspecific low back pain from 2005 to 2026. After reading this article, we believe that the recommendation against routine spinal imaging in patients without alarm symptoms or obvious clinical history warrants additional, more nuanced discussion. The designation of low back pain as “nonspecific” is contingent on excluding identifiable structural pathology. However, several clinically meaningful diagnoses are not identifiable by history or physical examination and require imaging for accurate characterization and management.

items.title: US Deaths Caused by Law Enforcement
items.summary: To the Editor A recent Research Letter provided important national evidence on long-term trends in deaths caused by law enforcement. The study, which reported an annual percent change (APC) of 3.5% (95% CI, 2.9%-4.2%) among adults and 5.6% (95% CI, 2.7%-8.7%) among children, concluded that the relative increase in pediatric deaths exceeded that of adult deaths. However, this comparative interpretation warrants further clarification.

items.title: Review of Low Back Pain—Reply
items.summary: In Reply We appreciate the letters by Dr Grenier and Dr Yahanda and colleagues about our Review on low back pain and welcome the opportunity to clarify 2 aspects of our recommendations.

items.title: US Deaths Caused by Law Enforcement—Reply
items.summary: In Reply Drs Sun and Wang and Ms Vadher and colleagues provide thoughtful replies to our Research Letter about deaths caused by law enforcement in the US. Their letters add important context for interpreting these trends and highlight opportunities to strengthen the public data available to study deaths caused by law enforcement.

items.title: Diagnosis of Suspected Pulmonary Embolism in Patients With Cancer

Although we welcome any strategy that limits CTPA in this population, the interpretation of this comparison, in particular of its control group, deserves scrutiny.

items.title: Signs, Both Clinical and Poetic
items.summary: In medicine, a sign is a patently observable manifestation of disease, such as jaundice or tremor. The poem “Signs” plays on the recognizable signification of illness, asking what happens when evidence of societal ills is everywhere in public view, but without diagnosis or remedy to follow. The anaphora of denial of the opening stanza, emblazoned on a literal sign posted on a clinic’s front door, first announces medicine’s constraints in treating the societal breakdown whose disease-like symptoms are so plainly seen. Yet other signs of malaise, perhaps more visible via poetry, abound elsewhere

items.summary: To the Editor The recent ACHIEVE-5 trial reported that the oral, nonpeptide glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist orforglipron, when added to titrated insulin glargine, lowered hemoglobin A1c by 1.03 to 1.08 (95% CI, 0.77-1.33) percentage points vs placebo at 40 weeks for both primary dosages (P < .001 for each). We would like to highlight the pancreatic enzyme data presented in eTable 7 in the article’s Supplement 1, which we believe were underrepresented in the discussion.
